evidence_quotes.quote: Finally, the authors inductively derived two subscales for measurement of identified domains in the social capital data and examined their relation to the respondents’ type of access to potable water.
Finally, everyone who was present in the area during the 2-week survey period was interviewed; no one directly declined.
These individuals connected other interested community members for an initial fee to this source of potable water by handmade pipe networks and sold water to them for a profit.
Seven community members could not acquire any water connection and instead had to buy water at a high price in buckets from others.

The main identified reasons for the failure or delay to obtain a connection are (1) a lack of information about the possibility and the long-term health and financial benefits of having piped water and (2) an inability to mobilize enough capital for the initial connection fee coupled with an absence of family or friends in the community who were willing to share their connection. Table 1 shows that the measured social capital is related to slum dwellers’ chances to meet their potable water needs.

The water supply case suggests that the number of accessed positions in the developed battery can be used as an estimate of individuals’ access through personal networks to valued resources such as unofficial information and finance and is also related to their social influence.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines slum residents' household/individual access to potable water in peri-urban Metro Manila, distinguishing an official direct utility connection, an illegal connection, connections to a neighbor's handmade resale pipe network (original or later, individual or shared), and having no connection (buying bucket water).
criterion_notes.c2: Fails both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study's exposure and central focus are the measurement of individual interpersonal social capital (personal social networks of acquaintances, friends, and kin across 16 occupations and 2 religious categories via a position generator), not a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor; although semistructured interviews briefly mention having 'good connections to the local authorities' as one of four personal assets helping one resident get an official utility connection, institutional or governance factors are not analyzed. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, the study clearly fails because it examines no rule-type mechanism governing water access (such as utility eligibility criteria, tenure or documentation requirements, administrative burden, regulated tariff/cost-recovery rules, official discretion, or enforcement), focusing instead on validating two position-generator social capital subscales against informal neighborhood water-sharing and resale outcomes.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary mixed-methods empirical data from a slum on the outskirts of Metro Manila (semistructured interviews in 12 neighborhood organizations and a face-to-face position-generator survey of 93 adults and household heads conducted in November-December 2006).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports potable water connection categories (official direct connection from the utility, illegal connection, originally connected or later connected to a community resale pipe network, and no connection) and water prices in Philippine pesos per cubic meter across social capital subscale scores (Table 1).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (individual adults and household heads in a peri-urban Metro Manila slum, N = 93 surveyed; n = 63 with water access data in Table 1), exposure (individual social capital measured via 18-item position generator subscales A and B), outcome (type of potable water connection and water cost per cubic meter), and study design (cross-sectional mixed-methods survey and semistructured interviews) are all clearly identifiable.

study_design: Cross-sectional mixed-methods field study (qualitative semistructured interviews and quantitative face-to-face social network survey validating a position-generator instrument)
population_and_sample: Adult slum dwellers and household heads on the outskirts of Metro Manila, Philippines: Phase 1 semistructured interviews with 23 leaders and 2-3 informants each across 12 neighborhood organizations; Phase 2 face-to-face survey of 93 respondents (66 adults on one street of 47 houses and 27 scattered household heads in the same organization; 63 cases reported in Table 1 water analysis)
exposure: Individual social capital (personal network access to 16 occupational positions and 2 religious groups, measured via position-generator Subscale A for common/local positions and Subscale B for rare/higher-prestige positions)
outcome: Type of access to potable water (official direct connection from the utility, illegal connection, originally or later connected to a neighbor's handmade resale pipe network, or no connection/buying water in buckets) and water cost in Philippine pesos per cubic meter
rationale: Excluded on Criterion 2 (E03: Wrong exposure). Although this empirical study in a Metro Manila slum examines respondents' potable water connection status and water costs (satisfying c1, c3, c4, c5, and c6), its exposure and methodological focus are the measurement of individual interpersonal social capital (personal network ties across occupational and religious positions using a position generator). It does not examine a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor under either the plain wording of Criterion 2 or the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading (no utility eligibility rule, tenure/documentation requirement, administrative burden, regulated tariff structure, official discretion, or enforcement mechanism is analyzed).
